There are various reasons why everyone wants to have lighting for camera work. My daughter and I have had a jewelry and pottery business we wanted to start but with everything going berserk two years ago, we put a hold on it all.

In the meanwhile, my perfect light that I love which goes on my camera shorted out. That made me frustrated. This light is larger, but I figured I can set it up on a tripod.

HOW THIS COMES
This comes in a box with a foam liner. There is a Type C connector for charging , a cord, and a screw on adapter for a tripod or on top of a camera if your camera can handle it.

CHARGING
This took me a while to charge it. After I left it in overnight, this was fully charged.

BATTERY
I purposely charged this up and did not use it for a few months. This battery was still up near 10 hours at 10% lighting on 5600K when I started it up. That is a great power retention. Using it, I get a few hours out of it before I recharge and I use it at less than 50% usually.

LIGHT COLOR
For all of the colors provided by this light, they are great. What I got it for, however, was jewelry and pottery photos so I am not going to be using the RGB lights very much except for advertising photos perhaps.

WHITE LIGHT COLOR
The white light color is kind of frustrating for me. I like to have natural lighting that does not add color to the photos. That means that in my situation, anything above 50% is too bright. This light only goes to 5600K in cool tones, but when I use it under 50% it still has some green/yellow to it. Yes, I can edit it out with color adjustments in my software, but it is a bit frustrating.

Some photos work out well, but others not so much. I do like a bit of yellow in my photos, so I will pull it down a little bit toward lower K value if I want warmer tones (aka sunlight type)

CONTROLS
The controls are easy to use and I like that it is mechanical and not software driven. The battery left is shown clearly and the settings are also lit up well.

WEIGHT
This is a heavy light. It is twice the size and weight of my other light so I can not put it on my camera. I use a tripod instead.

CASE
This does not come with a hard case which disappoints me. It has a cheap velveteen bag with no padding. It is nice, but you will need a case to keep this in for protection along with your camera.

THE BOTTOM LINE
This light is not bad. It give me some settings to work with on my jewelry. I would like it better if it was just a bit cooler in capability (higher K). As it is, I use it, but sometimes I find myself adding other lights to balance out the tint of this one.

MY RATING
FOUR STARS. This is nice, has nice battery capacity and retention of charge, but the light white color is not quite as nice as I was hoping for. It still is decent and I use it.

I got excited to see one of these small portable LED style ones that actually had a decent native resolution (most of them can accept 1080p, but are in reality only 800x600 resolution, or sometimes worse... 640x480!). This one is actually capable of displaying 720p of real dot resolution, which should make it at least as sharp as my Viewsonic and other traditional HD projectors. Ok, perhaps I'm spoiled, but I'm comparing this to our Viewsonic 720p projector that, to be fair cost me 3-4x as much.
And for the most part, it DOES work, however there are some caveats to its use. First of all, it doesn't seem as sharp as my 720p projector, even though it should have the requisite amount of dots. It's OK, its definitely better than the cheap 600p projectors, but something just isn't quite there when comparing side by side. It also doesn't get all that bright, but I suppose that's expected from the LED tech being used. You'll need black out shades or use it only during the night. Then there's the color- it isn't great. It works, but it has a cheap color reproduction that looks kind of flat and lifeless. Dark scenes sort of all blend together and become nearly impossible to see. It lacks the vibrancy of even an inexpensive television from decades ago. It gets the job done, but hardly the "theater experience" if you've been waiting to see that latest action/vfx film the way it was intended. It will look better on your TV at home, the only thing this has going for it is the large projection experience. For example, if you just want to give your kids a backyard movie night and don't care that the color and detail won't be as great as your indoor system, it will do the job on the cheap. I personally would not give up my mid-range projector for this one.
One thing that I found particularly annoying is that rather than the optical zoom and focus dials found on usual projectors, there is only a focus and tilt dial. No zoom. That means you have to physically move the projector closer or further to get it to reach the correct size you are shooting for. That actually got in the way of using it in a couple of specific places my other projectors can be used at optimal sizes.
That's not to say it gets everything wrong- I DO like that it is small and light and can even be turned on it's back to aim at the ceiling. That's something my big projector can't do, due to the airflow and cable management sticking out the rear. It also has a standard 1/4" 20 threaded tripod mounting point, so you can place this onto a tripod and get maximum mounting freedom. That will come in handy as I've always wanted to watch a movie in bed on the ceiling. But otherwise, don't think this projector will be as good as the other mid-rangers out there. This is still very much a low end projector. You'll have to spend at least 2-3x as much to get a decent home theater style experience, and much more if you want a high end one that will handle FHD/4k to get the real deal. This is more of a specialty use item.
Hopefully I won't need this, but feel better knowing my appliance is covered.

We have several networked devices in our house and also several individualized networks configured. Not all of the networks can be seen by all devices so I looked to this Belkin USB WiFi adapter to allow one of the older computer systems to access the most reliable network in the house - a 5GHz network that only one or two of the systems can see.

Installation was a snap. I popped in the CD, told it to install the drivers and we were off to the races. The particular target system was a 32-bit Windows Vista laptop. After just a couple of minutes the driver was completely installed and when I plugged in the USB adapter is was picked up immediately. I could see the desired network as well as several other networks in the neighborhood that were previously invisible to the computer. I shut off the built-in adapter, connected to the 5GHz network and went to the net.

So far, the connection has been very stable and speeds have been excellent. The router to which it is connected is a TP-Link router and so far we have seen no issues between the two devices. I have not had this adapter very long so it is still early to say it’s completely stable but all indicators up to this point have been very favorable.

Several other reviewers have mentioned that this adapter does not work with Linux. This is true - there are no drivers available for this adapter other than for Windows XP/Vista/7/8. If you need an adapter that will allow you to connect a Linux or Mac system to a wireless network, this is not the device you need right now.

So far I can’t find too much about which to complain concerning this router. It seems to be stable and reliable on the system to which it is attached here. I am satisfied with it and based on my experience with it can recommend it - if you’re sticking with Windows.

After a bad experience with another flat amp antenna I purchased the leaf for just over $50 .
It picks up 19 stations in the "low country" around a lot of tall pine trees.(20 is the max number of stations in a 60 mile radius here with any antenna according to the TV manufacturer).

You can paint the ant/ cables to match the walls. Comes with push pins for walls and Velcro for wall or window if you want them.Also has a plug into TV for the amp or you can plug into the wall like I did so it isn't hampered by the surge protector.

I get ABC, CBS,NBC,FOX,THIS,3 PBS stations, 3 Christian channels,a Spanish channel, WE,GET,MY,BOUNCE,YOU TOO, one music video channel and one other. The reception on all (but 2) is exceptionally strong with no blips in power even if you cannot put it in a window. I have mine hanging behind my curtain and most channels get 90-100% station strength almost constantly when 35%, even 30% will give you the station clear enough to watch a program with very few "blips" in reception.

I am enjoying not adjusting the Rabbit ear antenna (when I watched certain channels) even though it worked *good* enough for the money.

If you had another antenna before that only picked up 5-13 channels (for exp.) and you switch to a more powerful one like this, remember to unplug your TV a good minute before re- auto programming ( I forgot at first myself) as some TVs seem to "remember" how many it gets and stops at that number.

No need for an ugly outside antenna with this one.

When I use my hair dryer or turn on another "power draw", it doesnt get the interference the previous amplified antenna had, so probably uses less electricity, yet pulls in more stations.
I'm very happy with it. I get more channels than my basic cable had that I enjoy watching also.

I purchased two Fitbit Flex models, one for myself and one for my husband, on April 30, 2015. I didn't buy them from Amazon, but I did buy them from an authorized retailer. By October, my husband had quit wearing his because it wouldn't sync (we figured out this was easily fixed by restarting the phone the Fitbit app was installed on). He put his up and I continued wearing mine. During this time, my Fitbit started unlatching and falling off my wrist occasionally. I would find it laying around, or would notice, then retrace my steps and find the tracker. Fast forward to January: my Fitbit tracker fell off and was lost for good. I couldn't find it anywhere. I assume some lucky soul found it and calls it their own now. I started wearing my husband's tracker at this time with no issues. Then in March, it fell off my wrist in the parking lot of my office. I didn't notice this until it was too late. Someone I work with found it and returned it to me. Unfortunately, it was ran over by a vehicle (judging by the marks on the band) and crushed. No more Fitbit. Full disclosure: I tended to play with the fastener on my first Fitbit, though I made myself not do that anymore after losing it and using the second one. I also had 9 total bands with which I used the Fitbits in  this review. I though rotating between the bands daily would keep the fastenings tighter and reduce the risk of losing my Fitbit. Not so. When I decided to contact Fitbit and ask if they might be able to help me remain a loyal customer by giving me a percentage off my next Fitbit purchase, they obliged after a string of emails back and forth, sending me an email code to be used ONLY on their website. The discount was for 25% off, which is the everyday price on many of their items on Amazon. I should have pushed for more, but I didn't realize that until I went to compare their web prices with those on Amazon. In short, I feel like I dropped $200+ on Fitbit products and all of that money was lost. Their products with a watchband type fastener seem to be better, so my only caveat is that if you choose to buy the Flex, be prepared to lose it. I am currently without a tracker and have thought about buying one, but I am gun shy when it comes to dropping another $150 on a Fitbit Charge HR (has a watchband fastener) when I know the company doesn't stand behind their products. Sorry, Fitbit.

I have a couple of vertical mice that I use with my various computer systems, and they really do help with wrist fatigue and pressure. I also have a very nice Logitech MX Ergo trackball which is my go-to device for all of my systems. With Logitech releasing this vertical mouse, I was very optimistic that I would have the perfect solution. I was sorely disappointed. This is the worst Logitech device I have used and I can’t recommend it.

I’ll start with the good aspects of it, and then I will get into what isn’t so good.

This device can be connected via wireless USB or by Bluetooth. This is handy for when you want to use multiple systems and want to connect to them, in different ways. If you already have another wireless Logitech device, it can connect to the receiver for that device, reducing the number of wireless ports required. It connects well through either method and I have been able to move it between systems just with the press of the connection button on top.

In operation, it seems to work well as a pointing device. I will say that if you are not used to working with a vertical mouse there is a learning curve that is involved and you will be very frustrated while you make the adjustment. The movement isn’t hard – it’s working with the buttons which even though are worked with the same fingers they feel unnatural at first. This is a problem with all vertical mice, not just this one.

It is rechargeable, meaning no more batteries, and it holds a charge for a good while. I like mice and keyboards that don’t need batteries as in the very long term it saves money. (Logitech has a solar keyboard that is phenomenal and never needs to be plugged in at all – great device.)

I have three main issues with this vertical mouse. The first is the build quality. It feels very lightweight and cheap, and I would call it fragile. It is supposed to be light and maneuverable so it’s easy to use, but it’s so much so that it has a very cheap feel to it that is unsettling. Second, this is a HUGE mouse which for me is great but for most people is unworkable. It fits my hand very well, but I have hands like a gorilla. My wife tried it and found it to be completely unusable because she couldn’t work the buttons well at all due to the size. Finally, this is a very expensive peripheral compared to other vertical mice I have used that I actually prefer. This vertical mouse presently sells here for about $100. I have one that cost around $25 at the time I bought it, feels more solid and is easier to use. My wife and I compared the Logitech vertical mouse with my cheaper one, and we both agreed that the less expensive one was easier to handle and worked just as well. The only thing I lose with the cheaper mouse is Bluetooth connectivity, which in my case is not a deal breaker.

I wish I could rate this mouse more highly but I just can’t. It’s expensive, feels cheap and just isn’t made to fit smaller hands (and usually, it’s a challenge finding mice for larger hands). It’s worth consideration if you need a mouse that can be easily transitioned between wireless and Bluetooth, but if you just need to use it with one system I’d recommend researching other options before making a purchase.

One con is that it's not so kid friendly as the case is not actually a case, it is just the tablet design and it can easily be broken if dropped and not switched out. My biggest complaint is that it really kind of runs slow, especially when on youtube, it takes a while to load even with having excellent internet speed. So in turn my daughter gets frustrated and upset and doesn't want to use it. Also the past couple days it has been disconnecting from the Internet and having trouble reconnecting when no other device in the house is experiencing issues. It is decent for the price, we got it for 42.99, but we definitely prefer our kids fire tablet over this.
